fewshot.example_message: Imagine your 'you' from next year has come to visit, and guess what? You quit! How good is that?
Crumple a piece of paper into a ball and imagine it is your urge. Toss the "urge" into the garbage or against the wall. By doing this, you are letting go of your urges.

Pause. Notice the feelings you are having without judgement. Let them come and go. Being aware of your feelings means you can make a new choice about how you respond to your urges instead of smoking on autopilot.

fewshot.example_message: If you get urges, remind yourself that cigarettes did that to you. If you go back to them, they will keep making you suffer. Now you are breaking free.
How you would feel later on if you smoked during this social situation? Now think how good you'll feel for resisting!

When running a marathon, the hardest part is often towards the end, but many runners stick with it, knowing that the pain will pass. Learning to quit smoking is like running a marathon - if it gets hard, you may be closer to succeeding than you realize!

fewshot.example_message: Keep picturing yourself getting home later today knowing that you've gained a smoke-free day. It's nearly a reality!

Recent research has found that people who use self-talk when they try not to smoke (e.g. telling yourself 'you can do it') are more successful than people who don't. It might seem a bit strange, but talking to yourself like this appears to really help.

Imagine that your urge is a backseat passenger trying to distract you from reaching your destination. See if you can choose to keep driving instead of allowing your urges to distract you from where you want to go.
